## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vedabbajātaka* (Ja 48) is a narrative belonging to the Pali *Jātaka* collection. The framework story recounts that the Buddha delivered the tale while staying at Jetavana regarding an obstinate monk, warning him that his refusal to follow the advice of the wise had already proved fatal in a past life. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is the pupil of a brāhmaṇa named Vedabbha, who possesses an astrological spell capable of summoning a rain of treasure from the sky under a specific conjunction of the stars [Anandajoti 2010; Pye, Skillful Means]. When both are captured by bandits (*pesaṇaka-corā*), the Bodhisatta departs to procure a ransom and urges his master not to recite the charm in his absence [Barua 1921; Pye, Skillful Means]. Impatient and self-willed, the brāhmaṇa recites the spell and produces a shower of jewels, which incites uncontrollable greed among rival robber groups; the brāhmaṇa is murdered and the bandits slaughter one another until a thousand men meet their end [Anandajoti 2010; Pye, Skillful Means].

The concluding verse illustrates the perils of ill-gotten or immoderately used wealth, declaring that a fool who squanders fortune suffers later like a scoundrel who has shattered his water jar (*kuṭaṁ bhinno va dhuttako*) [Anandajoti 2010]. The *Jātaka* commentary includes the title in its chapter summary (*uddāna*) alongside nine companion tales [Appleton 2010]. Although discussed in modern studies as an illustration of means, the canonical context presents the story as an exemplification of misguided effort or "wrong means" (*anupāya*) rather than wholesome skillful means [Anandajoti 2010; Pye, Skillful Means].
